title: Nandi and Nahusha
hookLine: a boy becomes Shiva's own and a king of heaven becomes a snake, and Patanjali explains both
carry: as you act, so you become
tomorrow: the most generous king, in a well

lines: A KING OF HEAVEN KICKS A SAGE.
cards: The classical commentary on the Yoga Sutras names two stories together. The first is Nahusha, a good human king, made king of heaven while Indra is in hiding. The throne goes to his head.

He makes the great sages carry his litter like servants, and when the sage Agastya is too slow, Nahusha strikes him with his foot. Agastya says: fall, and be a snake. And the king of heaven drops to earth as a python.
The second is Nandi, a human boy who loved Shiva so wholly that he became Shiva's own.

teach.b: One went down, one went up, and Patanjali says it's the same law. Sutra 4.2: the change into another kind of being comes from nature overflowing.
Sutra 4.3: your deeds don't set nature moving; they only pierce the barrier, like a farmer. The commentary pictures him at a full canal. He doesn't carry the water to his field in buckets.
He cuts the little earth wall, and the water runs in by itself. Nature is already full. Your actions decide which wall gets cut.
Nandi's devotion cut one. Nahusha's pride cut another. Here's the Hindu teaching, in the Upanishad's own plain words: as you act, as you live, so you become.
Do good, become good; do harm, become harmful. That's karma, and the same Upanishad carries it into rebirth: what you're becoming doesn't stop at one body. Nahusha's story doesn't end in the dirt.

Ages later, in the forest, the python seizes Bhima, and Yudhishthira answers its questions about who is truly a brahmin. Not birth, he says, but truth, generosity, forgiveness, good conduct, kindness.
When the questions are answered, Nahusha is freed. Another wall cut.

teach.h: AS YOU ACT, SO YOU BECOME.
teach.b: And Nandi is still at his post. In Shiva temples his image sits facing the shrine, and in many of them devotees stop at Nandi and whisper their prayers in his ear, because he's the one who never takes his eyes off Shiva.
That's the farmer's lesson at both ends. You don't make the water. You choose the channel, and you turn into what you keep doing.

how: In Shiva temples an image of Nandi faces the shrine, and in many of them devotees bow to him and whisper prayers in his ear; Hindus teach that what a person does shapes what they become, in this life and the next, and teachers of the Yoga Sutras use the farmer of 4.3 for how deeds work.

o: a field watered by hand, one bucket at a time
a farmer: practice just cuts the wall, and nature flows
the effort that pushes nature to change shape

games.q: up, down, and the farmer — tap the pairs.
p: pride turned a king into a python
cuts the wall, lets nature flow
as you act, so you become

s: 4.3 says deeds push nature into a new shape
they only pierce the barrier; nature does the flowing.
Nahusha became a snake after striking the sage Agastya
and was freed ages later by Yudhishthira's answers.
in many Shiva temples, people whisper prayers into Nandi's ear

games.q: a friend says karma is just cosmic payback, a prize or a punishment handed down from outside. what does today's teaching add?
o: nothing: karma is a judge handing out sentences.
what you keep doing shapes what you become, the way pride made Nahusha a snake.
karma only applies to kings and sages.
games.why: the Upanishad: as you act, so you become. Patanjali's farmer: deeds cut the wall, and nature flows into the new shape. Nandi's love made him Shiva's own.

practice: Picture Nandi before the shrine, facing Shiva, steady. If you pray, sit the same way toward the form of God you love, and quietly tell one prayer, the way people whisper to Nandi.
If you don't, choose one quality you want to grow into, and face it. When the mind wanders, turn back and face it again, like the bull who never looks away.

wordCard.voice: Kshetrika, the farmer, from kshetra, a field. Patanjali's picture for how deeds work: they don't make the water, they cut the wall, and nature flows into what you're becoming.

orig.note: Sanskrit kṣetrika: a farmer, one who owns or works a field (kṣetra); the image of 4.3.

carryVoice: Your line: as you act, so you become. Nandi faced Shiva and became his. Day four hundred eighty-one, done.
